blocks.x: We can start off and give you a name again so we'll have it identified.
My name? Yes. Go ahead.
Go ahead. Let's start.
This is Charlie Love's story about Papa D. Dada and through my travels. I was with the band in Alexander, Harry Walker's. Harry Walker's.
You were talking about those trips you made in the rich guys that hired the band?

Yeah, rich fellas from Alexander, old man, Wade, Bred Clark, and Charlie Clark. They picked up old man, Dr. Williams in Monroe. He was a flute player, you know, in his early days. He's a rich man too, Dr. Williams, and he loved that band we had. It was a good band, you know. He said, well boys, we're going to give you all a chance to make some money. So they had a lot of old fellas, old sawmill men, you know, on the train. I didn't know them so well, the more than what they told me. But they had to sleep, you know. And them young fellas, them young sawmill men, they're full of definite, you know. They said, now you all got the set right in here. There's everything in here you want, whiskey, sandwiches, oranges. And say, we going to, we going from here to Baton Rouge. They had left from Alexander, going to Baton Rouge. And say, you all have to get up in the morning around 7 to 8. Sleep all you want. And say, all you got to do now, we going to give you a break to make some money. Just sit in here. Every 15 minutes you got to make a round. So you got to start the playing here. And play it to the end of the train. So you don't need that. All them drums, if you can't play them that way, say, just use the bass drum. And say, just make all the noise you can. We don't want you to play nothing but hot time in the old town tonight. Man, all of them was full of liquor, you know. Just having their fun. And say, every 15 minutes, who got a watch? It said, I have a watch, the leader, you know. Say, well, you look at your watch, you see. You play the back end of the train and play back. But play the same thing all the time. Hot time in the old town tonight. And say, you come back and you sit down and look at your watch when 15 minutes pass. Do the same thing. Don't care what nobody says. It's going to do like that. You get paid. Don't worry about that. So here we go. I mean, hot time in the old town tonight. And you get to the back of the train, turn around and come back. Man, the fellow just beating the bass drum. That fellow special to wait on the band, you know, Dan Tucker was his name. He could play a little carnage, you know, just a little. But he was there just to beat that drum and wait on us, you know. Just kept about four or five tubs of beer. Man, all the whiskey, man. We was having the time. Them fellows up in their boys' sleep, them old men, you know, after a while they got tired, you know, they said, for Christ's sake, don't come back here no more. And them fellows just laughing. Keep them awake, you know, them old fellows. They want to go, you know, and they want to show them there was no man, you know. Man, that tickle me. Yeah, we go sit down, you know, smoke, take a few beers, you know, start off. Hot times in the old town tonight. Man, them fellows were so tired when they got down here, them old men, you know. And something happened, we had to stop up in Carlton with the train, you see, until they find a place down there. Well the fellow said, if y'all want to go to town now, boy, says, y'all can get ready and go on up in the city, but the coaches will be right at the shade, the car shade, at the Union Station.
Yeah.

I said, all right. Say, I guess you boys, we won't see y'all until the head report up at the Greenwald Hotel, used to call the roads at the Greenwald. Report every morning because they didn't know exactly when they'd leave, you see. They didn't want us to get mixed up. So, I come out on the platform and this fellow, I tell him, old man, Miles, he didn't know how to tie his necktie, you know. He wanted to tie it like this. And you see him, I'm tired, yeah. He said, can you tie that boy? I said, yeah, tie my tie for him. I tied a tie for him, you know, and look in the glass, he looked at me. He said, that's fine, that's just fine. And on his hand, his pocket, give me $5. I said, gee whee, them fellows is giving us a break. Yeah. And here come this Dr. William. He said, Ed, get one of your boys there and put this sign out. Man, it was long as the coach was, you know. And they had ropes on it, a sea grass rope. Ed tied that in on the train, I tied this in, you know. Tied tight, put a swamp knot in it, you know, so you could just pull it and get it down. It says Monroe Boost Club.
Monroe Boost Club, huh?
Boost, Boost, I don't know what it's called. Boost Club. Boost. Boost. Like you're boosting something.
Boost.
Boost.
Like boosters or something.

Yeah, Boost. Monroe Boost Club. Boost. He gave me and Ed five dollars a piece to put that sign on both sides of the coach. And so he said, well, y'all get ready to go. Mr. Williams, that's the one. Dr. Williams. He said, well, y'all go into town? I said, yeah, we're going to run up town. Other boys didn't know nothing about New Orleans, but I knew, you see. Sure. He said, we're going up to Ramport Street. Well, the coaches will be there. You won't have to come back up here and call them. They'll just go down to Union Station and say, Dan Tucker will have the beer cool in the baggage car. That's why y'all have y'all fun. If you got any friends, just bring them aboard and give them some beer and let them have their fun with you. Yeah. And let them have their fun with you. And they said, well, Dr. Williams, I said, well, you all go into town? Yeah, we're going to town. Dr. Williams, I said, I'll bring it up here about this evening sometime when Ed Williams was going to see fit that we can come. You know, they want to hear our band play. Frankie Duesen and all them, Connors and Peter Bocas and all them. They're always on Ramport Street, you know. So we go down and the coaches was in. We get some bull there and started drinking, you know. And got our band in the baggage car and we start to practice. You know, that band used to practice every time they get a chance, every day. Man, we was in there practicing. You think we was playing for somebody. Yeah. Man, here come Frankie Duesen looking at him and I said, hello Frankie. Hello, you big ass so and so. Yeah. Oh, he's a nasty fella, you know. He said, look at that, look at that, Pete. Look at that little old big ass fella there. Remember Bunny in there with us on the train that day and us killed him? And after a while, here comes Joe Howard. Man, less time than about a half hour, the all was there. We got him a bull, you know, and fill him up with liquor. Cigars and everything. We ain't, oh, them old fellas used to throw some money away. And Ed had to go every day at nine o'clock find out when they left. We stayed down there four days. Oh, yeah. Doing nothing. Just practicing and playing on me.
Having a good time, too.

Man, I made so much money. Dr. William give us $20 a piece to have fun with. I didn't know what to do with money then. I just put pocket that money in. I had some fun, but I didn't know nothing about spending no big money then. So we had a time. Frankie and all of them come down and enjoyed themselves. Man, so one morning, the first morning, Ed went down to see when they were going to leave. He said, all right, Ed, say, have everybody aboard for about 11 o'clock. He said, just get on the train and you know where you all sleep at. Just go on to bed because we don't know what time. We're allowed to run around there and go on to many. So we got our orders and we run all around and ramp all the streets everywhere where we want to go. I come down about nine o'clock. We all come down tired, you know, went to bed. And they left when they, let's see, we slept in the baggage car. They put a whole lot of cots in that baggage car. That's the way it was. Every man had a cot of his own. And I had a train back out there and started running. I hadn't been home in a long while in Plagman. I owned a C Plagman up there. I ain't never woke up. When I woke up, they woke me up in Alexander. All the way. Yeah, and then got on the mountain. They changed the engines at Baton Rouge Junction, but it didn't change the course. Just the engine. Pulled out on the mountain, see from the teepee to the mountain. When I woke up, I was in the Alexander. Got off and went right on home. Yeah. Rest, went down to Lee Street that evening, you know. When we got in Monroe, it was day, that's the way it was. And Dr. Williams paid off. Says, fellas, y'all sure didn't have a nice band. We stopped in Baton Rouge, took Johnson and all them, got on board and we traded them there. I believe, let me see, we was two days in Baton Rouge. We give a dance there, that's the way it was.
We stopped over there. The whole club and everybody. No, the band.
Just the band.
Yeah.

We didn't have nothing to do, we had to make a parade in Baton Rouge and bring them fellas down to the hotel. And we was through, you see. Took Johnson and them come aboard, and I got Took to fix the dance, you know. We played dance. Made nice money on that. And from Baton Rouge we come to New Orleans, you see, and back. Back to Monroe, the paid us off in Monroe. And man, you know, they didn't have no liquor in Sreeport. All of us got us one of them big, there-go baskets and bought beer and different stuff, you know. Put it in the baggage car.
Mm-hmm.

He brought that in there. But shortly after that, man, they passed the city ordinance. He couldn't bring no liquor in Sreeport, not over a court. Like, you got a coronet or something like that, a detective get on there and say, you got liquor in there? No, sir. Open it up. He opened it up, you know. I said, I got a court in there. Where you get that Monroe? All right, they lie to have a court. That was during Prohibition though. Yeah. If they catch you with any more than that though, yeah.
Tell where you got it from or go to jail.

Ed Williams was a sharp fellow, the fellow who was the leader of the band. He had a big house with all the musicians, just a room there with him. He'd give parties, you know. And he had that liquor hidden around there. See like I lived there, I'd order me a court from Monroe. That's mine, you see. When he'd come I'd give it to him, see. The guitar player, he'd order a court. He'd come and give it to Ed. All of us have our own whiskey, you know. You'd have about seven eight quarts of whiskey in the same house. They never did look for it or nothing like that. They know we were musicians and they'd like to have a court. But a funny thing one night though, they caught me with a pint of the lid and they'd have a pint of liquor on Texas Avenue. They'd pass the city ordinance if you have any liquor like that you had to drink it up. If you didn't drink it up, they'd put you in jail. And if you'd drink it up and got drunk, they'd put you in jail. The police would have caught me, you know. And I had been drinking but I didn't have a whole pint, about a half a pint in a pint, you see. Searched me. Grab against that plant. I got up. Searched me. What's that? You got liquor, huh? I said, where'd you get that from? I said, it come from Monroe. I said, you know. Well, you know, you got to drink up that evidence. I was pretty high then, you know. I didn't want no more. I just had it in my pocket, you know. You see, you got to drink up the evidence if you don't. What you got left, that's the evidence against you. I'm going to arrest you. I said, all right, sir. Give me a little time. I took the bottle out, you know. He said, go ahead, start on. I said, nipped it a little bit and looked at it, you know. He said, uh-uh. Get busy. I said, get busy. I said, all right. I said, I don't think I can drink all. I'll have to rest. I said, well, if I drink it all, you ain't going to rest me? He said, no, I'll let you go if you drink it all. I looked at it again, you know. I said, I'm going to carry it all the way this time. Gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck, gluck. I said, throw that bottle out there. I said, you sure can drink. You can drink some liquor. I said, now get on off. I said, if you don't walk straight, I'm going to put you in anyhow, you know. And I buttoned my coat up, good, you know, like that. Pulled my hat off, you know, and started off kind of slow, you know. I said, good night, Cap. Man, I started to run, and I had to run. I couldn't walk straight. I'd have done that way. I said, good night, Cap. And when I got way down on Sprague Street, you know, I heard him laughing. Quack, quack, quack. I was laughing to keep from falling, you know. I was running to keep from falling. I said, oh, tickle that policeman. He seen me the next day, he said, I don't want to catch you with no more liquor now. I said, you can drink some liquor, Sam. I'm going to put you in jail if I see you with him. They would stick around there.
That was in Shreveport.

You know, they had a set of teenage boys there. They got a little junction before you get to Shreveport on the teepee, you know. The train goes halfway around, turn around and back into Shreveport, you see. And them fellas coming from Monroe, they got kind of strict on that liquor business that searched. They had caught a fella with a bass violin full of liquor, you see. And that run along, run along, when them teenage boys had a gang. They'd get together and they'd go out to the junction and play detective, you know. There was no detective. They'd go out there and confiscate a lot of liquor from them people, you know. That your grip up there? The fella said, yeah. Get it down, open it up. The fella opened it up, give me the grip. Confiscate that liquor, bring it to the city hall. That your grip up there? The fella said, no, I ain't got no grip. You get it down and look in it anyhow. It would be hit for the fellas sometime, you know. You'd look in there and you'd find the liquor and the fella disowned it. Well, he couldn't rest it. He just confiscated liquor, just take it. Put it in an automobile. We was waking at the Starfield, you know, them teenage boys. Here they come. Y'all want to make a little hot shot tonight? That's what they call it. Just go out with them and play a little music on the side road out the city. I said, yeah, how much in it? I said, what y'all charge? About three hours. No one of those big bands, this one was a cornet and a fiddle, a guitar, something like that. I said, about $15 a man. I said, all right. We'll come by and pick you up in the fold. What time do they get off? We'd be on duty. We'd be off at 10.30. They'd come around and pick us up. Go around through town, pick some other fella up and out they go. They know where they're going, you see. The other fella, the other girl, they go around and steal them girls out the house. And bring them out in the woods then, man. And get out there, man. They'd have a tour of the bands. They'd run off the highway way down on the side road. They had a regular picnic out there and some of them would go by the drugstore and bring the ginger ale and mix alcohol and whiskey and everything. Oh man, they'd have the time and they'd get to fighting, you know. They'd fight and everything. And they'd say, how much you charge to play another hour? I'd say about three dollars. We'd play another hour for you for three dollars. Beansbury out there already, you know. We'd keep that job, you know. We'd make plenty of money on them fellas. And now them fellas pay that, you know. The fellas say, you better pay us off. Now I say, because you all might get drunk and we don't get our money. Yeah, we'll get it up. They'll get the money up. We'll pay another hour, you know. Then after they get enough, get tired and everything, while we come home. About once or twice a week we'd have them jobs. But we didn't know what them fellas was doing. We found that out after. They broke it up. They caught a lot of them. We thought they was buying that liquor or something like that. It was playing detective. Hijacking that. Yeah. That musician sees some funny things.
Yeah, they sure do. You were telling me one day about that band you were playing in. I don't remember who else was in it when Punch came and sat in with you. Who?
Let's see.
Where was that?
Was that in the city? Yeah, let's see. Punch. Oh yeah, you were speaking about Hutchison.
Who was that fella?

That was a fella named Hutchison. He was a swell musician. He was a British, Honduras fella. He'd come here to New Orleans on a visit, you know, and stayed around and at the same time he wanted to play, you know. He didn't have no instrument with him. He was a baritone player. He learned how to play good in school. He was a fine musician. He said, if you got a mellophone anywhere around you, the fella said, yeah, we can get you one. Me and Willie Umphrey had a little band together, then Walter Pichon on the piano. So he sat in with us with that mellophone. Willie was one that said, what you going to do with that? He said, that's all right. He said, hand me a saxophone partner. He said, what kind of sax? Altos sax. Willie was playing a clarinet, you see, wasn't he used to, he could play ten or two, you know.
It was young Willie. Young Willie.

Young Willie. So Willie said, you going to play saxophone part on that thing? I said, yeah. I said, wait a minute, I want to see that. Hutchison sat down there, you know, and we had music. He said, you all got any music? I said, yeah, we hand him the mellophone, hand him the mellophone. He said, what part do you want? He said, give me the alto sax part. Give me the alto sax part. And I picked up and started off. Man, that boy played one of the sweetest mellophones I ever heard. He put his hand in it and everything, you know, getting them different tones. And they said, I wish you had a baritone I could play that. Well we didn't have no baritone. But the next night this fellow got killed, that guy. He had his baritone, just had made a funeral, you know. And he gave him that. I wish you had a boy to play that baritone. In the orchestra.
Who was that that just got killed? A musician?
Yeah, Butler Rap is his name. His name, they called him Guy A. Oh sure, yes. Yeah, Walter Beck who killed it.
Yeah, I remember. I wasn't here, I heard about it.

So the boys come in and sat in one night with me, you know. Get up, love, let me play you something. Get my lip waked up, yeah. I got up, you know. But first somebody, Louis the man, came in first, you know. He'd come in and say, want to rest you up? I said, yeah. That's one of them jitney dancers. He sat on there and played about an hour. I went off and got caught and come back and everything. And Hudson's sitting right there looking at them, you know, differencing the musicians. I come back and sat down, you know, before I could get a chance to play again, here come Punch you know.
Get up.

Punch took it. He had to go. Don't call that panamore you know. And Hutchinson was laughing, you know. He done played panamore too. He come from down that way or something. He was laughing at Punch you know. Nah, Punch. No, there was somebody else playing. Here come Punch, that's the way it was. Punch cut loose there with some wire around you know. Hudson got up and said, well, music is going to hell. And shortly after that, Manuel Moneta got a job next door with Butcher Fernandez's place. Him and Benji was partners, you know. But they hired Hudson over there to play alto. He got an alto.
Nice little band over there. Chattron trumpet.

They had a pretty fat band over there. Hudson got drunk one night. He seen them trombone players, you know, how bad they play and everything. And he seen a couple of them funerals there. That's where I got my kids. He come over there and told him, the fella said, give me that trombone now. Earl Humphrey, give me that trombone. Let me show you how to play a trombone. Earl handed me the trombone, you know. You talk about blasting. He went to blasting, making everything, you know, all out of key and everything. The fellas laughed at him, you know. He was high that night. I'll show you all how to play a trombone. Looked like he said, if you're going to make something, make something. You know, make some noise showing up. Oh man, that boy tickled.
I think you told me he said he was going to give up music, was it? When he said music's gone to hell after your-
Yeah, he said music's gone to hell.
That's after you heard Punch with all the wild runs. He went on back home. That's after you heard Punch play all those wild runs.
Yeah, Punch was a punch now.
He'd play some fancy stuff those days, I guess.

He'd make some funny stuff on the corner. The band playing something, he'd play Yankee Doodle or anything. And it'd come out right, you know, but it sounds so peculiar. Man, he cut loose there, you know, and he missed a few, you know, them high notes, you know. Hutchinson looked at him and said, well, music is gone to hell. And the next week he went home. He left here.
That was at the Taxi Dance Hall. Was that over on Iberville or?

That was on Iberville Street, yeah. They called him Beansy. His name is Edwin Fouye. Him and Butchie Fernandez were partners. He looked like a white man. He looked like a white fella. He's still around.
Is he the one who has the Astoria Hotel?
Well, Braden used to have that and he was about to lose it and Beansy saved him. Beansy had pretty good money.
Yeah.
Why they call him Beansy? He run a Beansy place. Used to sell beans and rice, you know. Oh really?
That's why?
He got rich selling beans.

I always heard he did a lot of gambling or ran gambling. Well, he was a real gambler. You know what a percentage of it is. But he made money out of selling red beans and rice, huh? Yeah. I didn't know. We must interview him someday too. We'll try to see him.
Call him Beansy.
Now his older brother, he's the one that invented the Zornings they put on his house. Oh, is that right?
Yeah.
My brother, he's got... He's got... He's got...
He's got... He's got... He's got... He's got... He's got... He's got... He's got... He's got... He's got...
He's got...

He's got... He's got... For him... Beansy. You work for him during World War II. After I first walked all my shoes out going around the WPA office and things. That's where I land that job in the Navy Yard. I'm waiting in that Navy Yard now and nothing but a baby kid. That's the time I was playing music with Tom Alvors.
Oh yeah.
And Eddie Benson. We used to practice right over the way from the gate.

Well, I think we only have a couple minutes left. Can you tell us anything about Eddie Vinson? Because naturally he's dead and we'll never learn much about him, but people like you could tell us a little about him.
He was a good musician. He could play pretty well. When I was a kid when I first met him, you see, him and Tom were always together. They lived in the first house down that land.
John Soxland, John Soxland they call it.
Well, that's where we used to practice. Not once a week, every day.
That's over in Algiers. Over in Algiers. Is it what they call down the coast there?

Down the coast, right at the Navy Yard gate, that west gate. It's right across the street. They got a little church on the corner. And they got a big house back in there with reed canes all around. You can't see it. It's falling down. They got a fellow living there, a rich man. They call him Mr. Ward.
Still there now.
Still living there.
And that's where Eddie Vinson.

Right across the street is the little double house back in the yard. That's where Eddie used to live. Eddie Vinson and Tom Alvin on one side. Oh I see. And I used to go down there and join them every day. They had the bass violin player they called Teep. And when I first come down there I could play the bass. I was a little bit of a fellow. But Tom wanted the cornet playing. He said, get your cornet. We'll all show you. And Eddie Vinson played a vowel trombone you know. And he drilled me through what we were going to play. And then lieutenants would yell at us over in the yard. They didn't have but one building there. And I waked on that building. I was waking. Nothing but a kid. So they used to hear us practicing over there so they hired us one Saturday night to give a dance out there. And we played such good music. So they gave us three nights. Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. And I got busy on the horn and I was taking lessons from everybody. I used to go around to old man Allen's house. Son wasn't born then. And I used to go around. George Hooker used to play cornet in the band. I'd get George to teach me what he knew. I'd go around the baritone players house. George Simms. He would teach me using fine musicians. And every time Charlie the Virgis they called me. Oh yes. Fess I think took lessons from him too. Yeah. And Pete. And me too. I went around and got some of them lessons. Play for nothing. All I want to do is to blow the horn and play. Man I got good. Then me and Tom come into playing down in the platinum parry where all them mosquitoes at. I got good you know and I wanted my pa and them to hear me at home. He said I wasn't going to play no cornet you know. I was a little bit of boy because I wouldn't play soft. I used to play too loud you know. So he told me, he said I ain't the way to study music. Learn how to get a tone and play soft. If you play soft you can play loud when you want. Well that's the fact. So I was playing pretty fair. I wasn't playing all that good when I went home. But he thought it was great. And he said that's my boy. That's son my boy. I went up there with Frankie Duesen and Peter. Joe Oliver on the cornet. Joe Oliver. They had a dance at my home at the Artfellas. I went up there and wake all day with them fellas for nothing. I wasn't getting paid. I just wanted to play with them. Just wanted to learn. My pa was proud of me too. He wouldn't let me come back down there. I had to stay home. Really? Yeah he went and got him a trombone and said you're going to play cornet now. And we had a little band at home they called Love's
office. Well yes you told me about that once you had your own band. That's the time Clarence

Williams' brother played the bass in the band and George Lewis. A fella in the name of Buddy Brunson. That man had the funniest lip I ever seen. I don't know what kind of trombone that he had. An E flat tenor trombone or something. A high one, a little one. Yeah. With the valve. With the valve. And he didn't know even how to tune but he could play it. You know what he'd do? He'd sound the air on the violin you know. And he'd finger any one of them valves, and he'd be flat that way he'd blow it up. He'd say, and blow it up a half tone without singing nothing. What is his name now? Buddy Brunson. I said I wonder what kind of fella is this. He just blew the horn naturally. It'd be out of tune and he'd blow it on up to tune. That was a powerful lip. And then he played good but he was what you call a tailgate man. He used to come down here and hear these fellas trombone playing and come right back up there and do the same thing. You'd get in the band and the instrument when they ain't tuning, he'd say that's alright, I'll tune it. He'd go, baaahhhhhh. He'd go right on.
I want to ask a little bit about Vincent again. How did he play? Did he ever take the slide trombone later? Do you remember?

At that time when I was practicing with him he played a valve trombone. But he could play that thing. He used to take a solo on it you know. Was he a good musician? Could he read and all? Yeah he could read right now. I hadn't started reading then when he was reading. I used to wish that I was great like him. And finally I got out of the business. My cousin named Brittany Henrietta, her husband was a bass horn player you know. He the one that taught Eddie Jackson. And he told me where to go to to get some good lessons. George Williams used to stay right by the bureau in Algey, the old bureau. He used to winter, when he'd come off the show, he was a trick trombone player you know.
Oh yes, I've heard of him. That's the end of it. That's right. That's right. Thank you.
